column15: This column represents a classification, cell-by-cell, at 0.005° resolution (55m), of the risk of ecosystem change in the cell due to the concurrency of biodiversity, phenological, anthropogenic, environmental, and climatic stressors. Each stressor was a variable defined on one of the variables in the previous columns, after standardisation and inversion (when necessary), so that high values for the variable corresponded to either harmful or fragile conditions. In particular, higher density change in land imperviousness was a harmful condition; tree density cover was a fragile condition (areas with many trees should be preserved);  loss of tree cover density was harmful; grassland presence was fragile (green areas to be preserved); grassland loss was harmful; high productivity by plant phenology was fragile (productivity is to be preserved); temperature increase was harmful (global warming is harmful); potential evapotranspiration loss was harmful (less water resources available is harmful); precipitation decrease was harmful (increased aridity is harmful); high species richness was fragile (biodiversity is to be preserved); land use increase was harmful (anthropogenic modifications to the territory are potentially harmful). Some categorial variables were re-interpreted with values between -1 and 1 to reflect these conditions. The ecosystem risk classification, according to the "Ecosystem risk classification according to a Variational Autoencoder with a later application of a Multi K-means process", calculates risks through a two-step process. In a first stage, a Variational Autoencoder is applied to the stressor variables to identify those with the lowest reconstruction probability. The vectors with reconstruction probability lower than the 50th percentile of the entire probability distribution are selected. Then, on this selection of vectors, a Multi K-means classification is applied: the process clusters the z-standardised stressor variables selected from the VAE through the iterative application of the K-means cluster analysis. Eventually, the process selects the clusterisation with the distribution of the vectors across the clusters that most resembles a uniform distribution. The clusters whose centroids contain the majority of values that are higher than the 50th percentile of the variable values across the entire dataset are classified as "at risk" clusters. Among these clusters, a subselection is made of the clusters associated with high centroid values for species richness and plant phenology productivity: if these values exceed two standard deviations from the mean across the cluster centroids, the cluster is classified as a "high risk" cluster. If these values exceed one standard deviation, the cluster is classified as "medium risk"; otherwise, it is classified as "low risk". This approach simulates the classification of similar ecosystem scenarios within anomalous conditions of the ecosystems, where anomaly is measured by the Variational Autoencoder reconstruction probability and similarity is measured through the Euclidean distance between the selected vectors of stressor variables.
